question.text: Loss aversion, as described in behavioural finance, means that:

answer.text: Monetary gains and monetary losses are felt with equal psychological intensity
Monetary losses hurt more than equivalent monetary gains feel rewarding
Investors are indifferent to losses provided long-term returns are positive
Investors prefer losses to gains because losses can be tax-deducted

explanation.text: The Logic: The workbook frames loss aversion qualitatively: monetary losses hurt more than equivalent monetary gains, and losses are described as significantly more powerful than gains in influencing investor behaviour. The Trap: Equal psychological weighting of gains and losses describes a purely rational utility framework, not the loss-aversion bias the workbook identifies. The tax-deduction and indifference options misread loss aversion as a deliberate preference rather than a bias. Note: Loss aversion is one of the cognitive biases discussed in the Portfolio Managers workbook's behavioural finance section.
